title: How Open Universities Australia modernized their data platform and significantly reduced their ETL costs with AWS Cloud Development Kit and AWS Step Functions
key_points: A small team replaced a licensed third-party ETL tool with Step Functions, Glue, Lambda, AppFlow and Redshift, all defined in CDK from a code repository.
Key pattern: Step Functions submits SQL (transforms, COPY, UNLOAD) to Redshift and polls for completion, so no Glue job or Lambda sits idle waiting for the warehouse.
Other patterns: API pulls in Glue Python jobs landed in S3 then COPY, AppFlow to S3 then COPY on a completion event, and reverse ETL via UNLOAD plus Lambda pushing to external apps.
services: AWS Step Functions, Amazon Redshift, Redshift Data API, AWS Glue, AWS Lambda, Amazon AppFlow, Amazon EventBridge, AWS CDK
decision: Licensed ETL tool vs code-defined Step Functions orchestration of warehouse SQL
attaches_to: aws-bytes: orchestration (later); Redshift ETL failure alert (planned)
authors: Open Universities Australia — Michael Davies, Emma Arrigo

title: Hybrid big data analytics with Amazon EMR on AWS Outposts
key_points: Runs EMR on an Outposts rack so sensitive data stays in on-premises S3 while being joined with public data from a Regional bucket, with Lake Formation controlling table access.
Niche hybrid-hardware scenario, off the reader's path.
services: Amazon EMR, AWS Outposts, Amazon S3 on Outposts, AWS Lake Formation, AWS Glue Data Catalog

title: How MuleSoft achieved cloud excellence through an event-driven Amazon Redshift lakehouse architecture
key_points: MuleSoft built an internal cloud-governance portal on Redshift: cost reports, Trusted Advisor checks and asset inventory land in S3, and new files trigger a Glue crawler plus ETL workflow through EventBridge and SQS.
Glue flattens nested JSON and pivots resource tags into columns so every asset gets an owner; Redshift reads the lake through Spectrum and serves Tableau from materialized views.

Practical caution: catalog partition counts grow fast, so a short retention window with crawler-driven partition cleanup keeps queries quick; views are refreshed by the event flow, with auto refresh under evaluation.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift Spectrum, Redshift materialized views, AWS Glue, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SQS, AWS Cost and Usage Report, AWS Trusted Advisor
decision: Event-driven Glue loads with pipeline-triggered MV refresh vs scheduled batch with auto-refresh for near-real-time warehouse reporting
attaches_to: aws-bytes: cost optimization (later); dbt-pipelines (materialized views on Redshift)
authors: MuleSoft — Sean Zou, Terry Quan, Audrey Yuan, Avijit Goswami, Rueben Jimenez

title: OpenSearch Vector Engine is now disk-optimized for low cost, accurate vector search
key_points: OpenSearch k-NN indexes can run in an on-disk mode that keeps compressed vectors in memory and rescores from disk, trading some latency for much lower memory.
AWS reports roughly a third of the cost of in-memory mode; vector-search feature, off path.

title: Access Apache Iceberg tables in Amazon S3 from Databricks using AWS Glue Iceberg REST Catalog in Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse
key_points: Databricks compute on AWS reads Iceberg tables catalogued in the Glue Data Catalog through the Glue Iceberg REST endpoint, so the table definition lives in one place.
Lake Formation decides what the Databricks role may see and hands out short-lived S3 credentials, after enabling full-table access for external engines.
Same-account setup on general-purpose buckets; S3 Tables works with a config change.
services: AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS Glue Iceberg REST Catalog, AWS Lake Formation, Apache Iceberg, Databricks, Amazon S3
decision: Separate catalogs per engine vs one Glue catalog exposed over Iceberg REST with Lake Formation credential vending
authors: Srividya Parthasarathy, Pratik Das, Venkatavaradhan Viswanathan

title: Generate vector embeddings for your data using AWS Lambda as a processor for Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion
key_points: OpenSearch Ingestion pipelines can call a Lambda function as a processor; the example batches records, gets embeddings from a Bedrock model and writes them to a serverless vector collection.
Search-pipeline feature, off the reader's path.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, AWS Lambda, Amazon Bedrock
authors: Jagadish Kumar, Samuel Selvan, Srikanth Govindarajan

title: Automate topic provisioning and configuration using Terraform with Amazon MSK
key_points: Creates, changes and deletes Kafka topics on MSK (provisioned or serverless) from Terraform instead of letting brokers auto-create them or editing them by hand.
Narrow infrastructure-as-code walkthrough.

title: How EUROGATE established a data mesh architecture using Amazon DataZone
key_points: A container-terminal operator publishes data products from separate accounts into a DataZone catalog so data science and BI teams can find and subscribe to them instead of building one-off connections.

Two producer patterns: IoT data from Kinesis via Firehose and a daily Glue job into an S3 lake, and on-premises application data moved by DMS (scheduled through Step Functions) into a central Redshift warehouse shared to consumer warehouses.
High-level story; DataZone has since been folded into SageMaker Unified Studio.
services: Amazon DataZone, Amazon Redshift, AWS Glue, AWS DMS, AWS Step Functions, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon SageMaker
decision: Point-to-point BI connections vs a catalog-based data mesh with subscription access across accounts
authors: EUROGATE — Dr. Leonard Heilig, Meliena Zlotos, Lakshmi Nair, Siamak Nariman

title: Juicebox recruits Amazon OpenSearch Service’s vector database for improved talent search
key_points: A recruiting-search startup combines keyword ranking with vector search in OpenSearch, uses exact k-NN scoring to compare embedding models, and feeds indexes through OpenSearch Ingestion.
Short search-product story, off the reader's path.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion

title: Batch data ingestion into Amazon OpenSearch Service using AWS Glue
key_points: Three ways for a Glue Spark job to bulk-load data into OpenSearch: the OpenSearch Spark library, the Elasticsearch Hadoop library, or Glue's built-in OpenSearch connection.
Glue is only the loader here; the subject is feeding a search engine, which is off the reader's path.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, AWS Glue, Apache Spark
authors: Ravikiran Rao, Vishwa Gupta, Suvojit Dasgupta

title: Cost Optimized Vector Database: Introduction to Amazon OpenSearch Service quantization techniques
key_points: Surveys ways to shrink vector indexes in OpenSearch (binary, byte, FP16 and product quantization, plus disk-based search) and the memory, recall and latency each trades away.
Vector-search tuning, off the reader's path.

title: Build a high-performance quant research platform with Apache Iceberg
key_points: Benchmarks four layouts of the same order-book data on S3 written and read by Glue jobs: plain Parquet vs Iceberg, each unsorted (partitioned only) and sorted on the time column.
Explains why plain Parquet layouts hit S3 prefix throttling and listing costs, and how Iceberg's metadata, hidden partitioning and object-store prefixes avoid hand-built salting.
AWS reports Iceberg reads up to 52% faster, about 32% fewer Glue DPU hours on the read jobs and 10-16% less S3 storage, with similar write cost; sorting raised write cost but sped up reads further.
services: Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue, Amazon S3, Amazon EMR on EKS, Apache Parquet
decision: Plain Parquet folders vs Iceberg tables, and partition-only vs sorted writes, for read-heavy analytics on S3
attaches_to: aws-bytes: File Layout Optimization (active); dbt-pipelines (Athena + Iceberg folder)
authors: CryptoStruct — Guy Bachar, Alex Tarasov, Boris Litvin, Jiwan Panjiker, Sercan Karaoglu, Salim Tutuncu

title: Use CI/CD best practices to automate Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster management operations
key_points: Keeps OpenSearch index settings and mappings in a repository and applies them through a pipeline, using either the Terraform OpenSearch provider or the Evolution migration library.
Infrastructure built with CDK, CodeBuild and Lambda; search-platform operations, off the reader's path.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Terraform, AWS CDK, AWS CodeBuild, AWS Lambda

title: Ingest data from Google Analytics 4 and Google Sheets to Amazon Redshift using Amazon AppFlow
key_points: Console walkthrough that connects Google Analytics 4 and Google Sheets to AppFlow through a Google Cloud OAuth client and lands both in tables on a Redshift Serverless workgroup.
Most of the effort is the Google-side OAuth setup and the IAM role that lets AppFlow run SQL through the Redshift Data API.
Glue's later native SaaS connectors now cover much of this ground, so it is mainly a reference for AppFlow as one ingestion option.
services: Amazon AppFlow, Amazon Redshift Serverless, Redshift Data API, Google Analytics 4
decision: AppFlow vs Glue SaaS connectors vs custom API code for landing SaaS marketing data in Redshift
authors: Ritesh Sinha, Amit Ghodke, Tahir Aziz, Raza Hafeez
